# ROS / ROS 2

You will meet [ROS](https://www.ros.org/) and [ROS 2](https://docs.ros.org/en/rolling/)
everywhere in robotics job posts, labs, and vendor SDKs. **Do not build new work on
them** for this tutorial’s stack — and treat “we should just use ROS” as a red flag in
research code unless you are forced to talk to an existing ROS-only robot.

[Do not adopt ROS or ROS 2 as your project middleware. Prefer plain Python (or C++)
libraries, files on disk (URDF/MJCF), and explicit IPC ([Inter-process
communication](inter-process-communication.qmd#inter-process-communication)) when you
need multiple processes. The ecosystem is a pain to install, version, debug, and
**port** across machines, distros, and cloud images.]{.common-bug-warning}

## Why it hurts

| Pain | What you actually hit |
|---|---|
| **Install / env** | Distro pins (`Humble`, `Jazzy`, …), system packages fighting `uv`/`conda`, “works on my Ubuntu” only |
| **Versioning** | Nodes, messages, and launch files bit-rot across distros; regenerating interfaces is busywork |
| **Portability** | Hard to ship a **single** reproducible research env; containers help, but you still carry the middleware |
| **Debugging** | Failures span launch, DDS/discovery, QoS, and your algorithm — stack traces stop being enough |
| **Abstraction tax** | Topics/services/actions for what could be a function call, a file, or a small ZMQ socket |

URDF as a **file format** is fine — see [Asset files](asset-files.qmd#asset-files). That
does **not** mean you need `roscore`, `colcon`, or a graph of nodes to move a joint in
MuJoCo or Motrix.

## What to do instead

- **Sim and control in-process** when you can: load MJCF/URDF, write `ctrl`, `step`
  ([Two simulators](two-simulators.qmd#two-simulators)).
- **Need processes?** Use the patterns in
  [Inter-process communication](inter-process-communication.qmd#inter-process-communication)
  (shared memory, ZMQ, …) with **explicit** message layouts you own.
- **Must talk to a ROS robot?** Isolate a thin bridge at the boundary; keep your
  training / control / research code ROS-free so you can still run headless and port
  environments.

This chapter is a policy choice for **clarity and portability**, not a claim that no
production robot ever runs ROS. Use ROS when the **hardware or lab already requires
it** — not as the default architecture for new learning or sim code.
